posts.title: Inside the Miller Residence: One House, Room by Room
posts.excerpt: A West Seattle whole-home project — two-tone cabinetry, brass carried everywhere, and a blue-green thread that ties forty-one photographs into one house.
posts.body:
The Miller Residence in West Seattle is the largest gallery on this site — forty-one photographs, kitchen through laundry room. That's deliberate. A single hero shot tells you what a kitchen looks like; a full set tells you whether a house was designed as one thing or decorated room by room.

Here's what we were thinking as it came together.

## The plan comes before the palette

The kitchen sits at the center of the main floor, open to dining and living, with the view held at the end of the sightline. Everything after that decision — where the island lands, how tall the pantry column runs, which wall gets the range — follows from the way the family actually moves through the floor: in the back door, drop everything, cook, eat, sit down.

We draw that circulation before we choose a single finish. It's the least glamorous part of the process and the part that decides whether the finished house feels effortless.

## Two cabinet finishes, doing two different jobs

The perimeter uppers are painted light, which keeps the ceiling height and the windows doing the work. The base cabinets and the tall column are warm wood, which grounds the room and gives the island something to talk to.

A two-tone kitchen fails when the split is arbitrary. It works when each finish has an assignment — light where you want the room to recede, wood where you want weight.

![Painted uppers keep the perimeter light; the wood base cabinets carry the weight.](assets/img/work/miller/miller-13.jpg)

## One metal, carried all the way through

Brass runs everywhere here: the faucet and pot filler, the cabinet hardware, the pendants over the island, the sconces in the baths, the shower set, the mirror frames.

The rule we use on every project: **pick one dominant metal and commit to it**, then allow a single accent if a room genuinely needs one. Three metals chosen room by room is the fastest way to make a well-built house look unplanned.

## A color that travels

Blue-green shows up at the island stools, on the living room walls, in the secondary bath, and again on the laundry cabinetry. Nobody walking through reads it as a scheme — they just feel that the rooms belong to each other.

That's the whole point of a whole-home palette. It isn't about painting everything one color. It's about repeating two or three notes often enough that the house holds together.

![The same blue-green that shows up at the island stools returns on the living room walls.](assets/img/work/miller/miller-19.jpg)

## Be quiet in some rooms so you can be loud in others

The kitchen backsplash is a calm stone. The guest shower is a lantern-shaped tile. The primary bath floor is a checkerboard. The laundry and mudroom floors are patterned.

Utility rooms are the best places in a house to take a risk. They're small, they're cheap to change, and they're where a little personality goes the furthest.

![Patterned floor tile and painted cabinetry in the laundry room.](assets/img/work/miller/miller-37.jpg)

## Why an architect ends up in your kitchen

Cabinet elevations, lighting layouts, and tile layouts all get drawn before anything is ordered. Not because drawings are fun, but because that's when a misaligned sconce or a pendant that lands three inches off the island centerline is still free to fix.

That's the difference between a designer's eye and a set of construction documents — we bring both, and the second one is what keeps the first one from getting expensive on site.

## See the whole house

The full set is in [Select Work](work.html). Photography by Emily Keeney.

If you're planning something similar — a whole-home remodel where the kitchen, baths, and the rooms in between all have to add up — [tell us about it](contact.html).

posts.title: The Strauss Residence: Traditional Detail, Working Hard
posts.excerpt: A furniture-style island, arches used more than once, and a green-tiled shower — how classic detailing makes a house feel current instead of dated.
posts.body:
Traditional detail has a reputation problem. Done carelessly it reads dated — heavy, fussy, a decade behind. Done with discipline it does something no minimal interior can: it makes a new house feel like it has been there a while.

The Strauss Residence is our argument for the second version.

## The island as a piece of furniture

The perimeter cabinetry is inset, painted, and quiet. The island is not — it's dark wood with turned legs and a stone top, sitting in the room like a table somebody moved in rather than a run of cabinets that happened to stop.

That contrast does real work. It breaks up what would otherwise be an unrelieved wall-to-wall kitchen, and it gives the open plan a center that reads as a room, not a corridor.

![The island sits in the room like a table somebody moved in.](assets/img/work/strauss/strauss-04.jpg)

## One shape, used more than once

There's an arch over the range and an arch at the opening into the dining room. Two instances, same family of curve.

A detail used once is decoration. A detail used two or three times in the same house becomes a language — the eye picks it up on the second appearance and starts reading the plan as intentional.

![The arched opening into the dining room answers the arch over the range.](assets/img/work/strauss/strauss-03.jpg)

## Cabinetry that goes all the way up

Running the cabinets to the ceiling is one of the highest-return moves in a remodel. You gain real storage, you lose the dust ledge, and — most importantly — the wall reads as architecture instead of furniture parked against plaster.

The long brass pulls do the rest, drawing the eye vertically and making a nine-foot wall feel taller than it measures.

## Two metals, two rooms, no confusion

Brass in the kitchen. Polished nickel in the bath.

That isn't inconsistency — it's the mixing-metals rule applied properly: **one dominant metal per room, carried completely**, rather than a little of everything everywhere. Each room reads as decided. Walk between them and you notice warmth in one and coolness in the other, which is exactly the intent.

## Color where nobody expects it

The shower is tiled floor to ceiling in a green glazed tile with enough variation that no two pieces read the same, and the ceiling above it is dark.

A small, enclosed, wet room is the safest place in a house to commit to a color. There's no adjacent furniture to fight, the tile is going in once, and the payoff — the moment someone opens that door — is out of all proportion to the square footage.

![Green glazed tile floor to ceiling, with a dark ceiling above it.](assets/img/work/strauss/strauss-05.jpg)

## Detail that reads from across the room and up close

The stair hall is paneled, with a white-oak rail and treads against white risers. From the entry you register proportion and light. From the third step you register the joinery.

Good detailing has to survive both distances. That's the standard we hold on every set of drawings that leaves the studio.

## See the project

The Strauss Residence is in [Select Work](work.html), alongside the rest of our whole-home projects.

Thinking about a remodel where classic detail has to feel current? [Start a conversation](contact.html).

posts.title: Design With Intent: How We Begin Every Project
posts.excerpt: Great spaces don't start with a mood board — they start with how you actually live. A look inside the questions we ask before a single finish is chosen.
posts.body:
Every project at Drift begins the same way: not with a paint color, but with a conversation about life.

## Function first

Before we shape a single sightline, we map how a space will really be used — where the light lands in the morning, where people gather, where the quiet corners need to be. Only then does the design work begin.

## The details that matter

From the placement of furnishings to the flow between rooms, we design for the way a home is lived in and remembered. The result is a space that feels effortless — dynamic where it should be, calm where it needs to be.

That discipline is what turns a house into a home, and a project into something lasting.

posts.title: Staging That Sells: Why Presentation Moves Markets
posts.excerpt: In today's market, buyers decide in seconds. Here's how elevated, strategic staging helps a listing show its best — and sell faster.
posts.body:
A beautifully staged home doesn't just look better — it *sells* better.

## First impressions are everything

Buyers form an opinion within moments of walking in (or scrolling past a listing photo). Thoughtful staging highlights architecture, warms up empty rooms, and helps buyers picture themselves at home.

## Strategy, not just style

We stage to the market and the buyer — curated furnishings, considered styling, and a flow that photographs beautifully and shows even better in person. It's design in service of the sale.

Ask us about our **Pay-At-Close** option, which lets qualifying sellers defer their staging investment until the home sells.

posts.title: Permit-Ready: Building Faster With Pre-Approved Plans
posts.excerpt: Our library of ready-to-build plans — including The Si Plan, pre-approved in the City of Everett — can shorten your path from idea to groundbreaking.
posts.body:
Building a home is a big undertaking. Starting from an approved plan can make it dramatically simpler.

## What 'Basic Plan' approval means

In the City of Everett, our **Si Plan** is approved as a Basic Plan — cleared to build on an expedited permit with no modifications required. That means less time in review and a faster path to construction.

## A plan for the way you live

Every plan in our library can be built as-drawn or tailored with modifications. We'll walk you through pricing for the plan as-is and for any changes you have in mind.

Browse the library and ask which plans are approved in your jurisdiction.
